Do you hear that? The constant gunfire? The shelling? And they tell the world there is a ceasefire? There is no pause. No reprieve. No safety for Palestinians in Gaza. On October 11, our team visited families whose tents had been burned, leaving them without shelter once again. Even as we filmed, heavy gunfire echoed around us. This is the reality of life in Gaza. Families who have lost everything continue to live under the threat of violence, yet refuse to be driven from their land. This is what steadfastness looks like. Sumud. A determination that is difficult to comprehend unless you understand what it means to face the loss of your homeland. They have burned their shelters, destroyed their neighborhoods, and displaced them again and again. But they have not broken their connection to Palestine. They are not leaving. They are not surrendering their right to exist on their land. Help support them. The Sameer Project is one of the only organizations that delivers aid in these danger zones. For decades, Israel has withheld Palestinian bodies in numbered graves and military freezers, leaving families unable to bury their loved ones or learn what happened to them. Since the war on Gaza began in October 2023, the issue has escalated dramatically, with thousands of people missing and the scale of bodies held by Israeli authorities still difficult to establish.   The National Campaign to Recover the Bodies of Martyrs says it has documented 805 Palestinian bodies held in numbered cemeteries and freezers, including 80 children. Separately, it cites around 900 bodies from Gaza whose identities, locations or circumstances remain inadequately documented.  But the issue goes beyond the numbers.  Families are fighting for answers through Israel’s courts, while a court-ordered DNA database intended to help identify remains has, according to campaign coordinator Hussein Shuja’iyya, still not been implemented by the military. The campaign also says bodies are sometimes returned just before court hearings, allowing petitions to be dismissed without a final ruling that could help other families.   Withholding bodies as bargaining chips, inadequate identification records and the lack of accountability raise urgent questions under international humanitarian law, which requires the dead to be treated with dignity and efforts to identify them and facilitate the return of remains to their families.
